insights: Required testing is back across nearly the entire top tier: MIT (2022), then Dartmouth, Yale, Brown, Harvard, Caltech, Stanford (Class of 2030), Johns Hopkins, and UT Austin all reinstated for the 2024-2025/2025-2026 cycles. For applicants targeting T20s, plan to submit an SAT or ACT — test-optional is effectively gone at this tier.

Policies are not identical 'required': Yale is test-FLEXIBLE (SAT, ACT, AP, or IB accepted), Stanford's requirement starts one cycle later (Class of 2030), and most schools allow narrow hardship exceptions. Read each school's exact wording.

The University of California system is the major outlier: fully test-free / test-blind since 2021 — scores are not considered at all. Korean families applying to UCs should redirect prep energy from the SAT toward the capped weighted UC GPA and the 8 personal-insight questions.

Mid-50% SAT at the very top is compressed and high: roughly 1480-1580 (Harvard ~1510-1580, Yale ~1480-1560, Dartmouth/Brown/Caltech ~1500-1580), with ACT 34-36. A score below the 25th percentile is a real flag at these schools; the practical target is the median (~1550) or above.

Common Data Sets do NOT publish a single 'average GPA.' Section C11/C12 reports GPA in BANDS (% with 4.0, 3.75-3.99, etc.) plus class-rank bands. At the most selective schools the top band is crowded — e.g., JHU reports 70%+ of enrolled first-years with a 4.0 and 90%+ at 3.75+; MIT reports ~99% of rank-reporting students in the top tenth.

Grade inflation is the explicit reason scores came back. ACT research shows average high-school GPA rose from 3.22 (2010) to 3.39 (2021) while ACT scores fell — a top-25% test-taker's average GPA climbed from 3.5 (2010) to 3.7 (2021). A 4.0 no longer differentiates, so admissions offices lean on test scores to compare applicants across high schools with different grading scales.
